prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Perhaps, Sunday, Florida

outputs.L1:
Perhaps it was just another break-in some years ago. Or perhaps it was the kind of charm that seduces suddenly, out of nowhere, though it has long been rehearsed—until you realize, too late, that half your living life has walked straight out the door, into the noonday glare of some godforsaken Sunday place. Somewhere in central Florida, the so-called Widow State you believed was safe—which, at the time, still remained obscure; so obscure, in fact, that it was almost dark when you awoke, so unlike yourself, as if in a manic haze, rifling through drawers for letters, tchotchkes, and so much else.

So you had suddenly been had.

There are times when human frailty lets down its guard. There is a ring of fire Dante numbered and named for those who prey upon the old. The children are grown and living elsewhere, and you are left alone, stumbling down the hall.

It could have begun as a friendly call. A friendly knock. A slight accent adding to the charm. A friend of a friend of a so-called friend, with no time to trace. That noonday glare of sunlight, like a halo, for the added touch.

Have you forgotten anything? Anything?
outputs.L2:
Maybe it began as nothing more than a burglary, years ago. Or maybe it was that spell of charm that appears without warning, though it has been practiced for a long time, and by the moment you understand what has happened, it is already too late: half of the life you were still living has slipped right out through the door and into the harsh Sunday noon of some forsaken place in central Florida—the “Widow State,” as people call it, the place you had believed would be secure. Back then it was still little known, so little known that when you came to, it seemed almost dark, and you felt nothing like yourself, as if caught in a feverish trance, tearing through drawers in search of letters, trinkets, and all the other things.

So, all at once, you had been taken in.

There are moments when ordinary human weakness stops protecting itself. Dante marked and named a circle of flame for those who exploit the elderly. The children are grown and settled elsewhere, and you are alone, unsteady as you make your way along the hallway.

It may have started with a pleasant telephone call. Or a polite knock at the door. Perhaps there was a faint accent that made the person seem even more appealing. Someone connected to someone connected to someone supposedly familiar—too many links to check in time. The bright noon sun could have framed them like a halo, giving the whole scene one more convincing detail.

Are you sure nothing has been overlooked? Nothing at all?
outputs.L3:
The text portrays an older person who comes to understand, painfully and too late, that they have been deceived or exploited. What may once have seemed like kindness, attention, or harmless companionship is revealed as manipulation. The realization arrives after the damage has already been done, making the situation feel especially tragic.

The setting adds to this sense of vulnerability. It evokes a lonely part of central Florida, described as an obscure and supposedly safe “Widow State.” This phrase suggests a place where many older people, particularly widows or widowers, live quietly and apart from the larger world. Although such a place may appear peaceful or secure, the text implies that isolation can create hidden dangers.

The speaker emphasizes how easily vulnerability can develop when people are alone, aging, and separated from their grown children. Without close family nearby, an elderly person may be more exposed to strangers who offer attention, help, or affection. Loneliness can make even a brief moment of warmth feel meaningful, and that emotional need can be exploited by someone with dishonest intentions.

The deception may have begun in an ordinary way: a friendly phone call, a knock at the door, or a charming stranger who seemed trustworthy. The person responsible may have used politeness, sympathy, or personal charm to gain access to the older person’s life. What appeared to be concern or companionship gradually became a means of control or theft.

The text strongly condemns those who prey on the elderly. It presents their actions as morally vile, not merely dishonest but deeply cruel. By comparing their wrongdoing to a punishment worthy of Dante’s hell, the speaker suggests that such people deserve severe judgment. Exploiting the old, the lonely, and the trusting is shown as one of the most shameful forms of betrayal.
outputs.L4:
At first, it seemed like kindness.

That was what made it so difficult to recognize. The voice at the door was warm, the smile practiced but convincing, the manner gentle enough to disarm suspicion. There was nothing forceful in the beginning, no raised hand, no obvious threat, no sudden break in the ordinary rhythm of the day. Instead, there was conversation. There was flattery. There was the slow, careful performance of friendliness.

For an older person living alone, such attention can feel like relief. A stranger who listens can appear almost providential when the house has grown quiet and the telephone rarely rings. A compliment, a shared laugh, an offer to help carry something or fix something or explain something—these small gestures can seem harmless. They can even seem generous. But beneath them, in this encounter, lay calculation.

The memory returns in fragments: a face at the threshold, a hand resting lightly on the table, papers shuffled, a purse opened, a drawer left ajar. There is the sound of a friendly voice saying, “Don’t worry,” and “You can trust me,” and “I’m only trying to help.” There is the confusion of trying to follow too many words at once, the embarrassment of not wanting to appear rude or forgetful, the fear of seeming ungrateful to someone who has shown unexpected interest.

Then comes the absence: the missing money, the vanished object, the signature obtained under false pretenses, the account changed, the confidence broken. What had felt like companionship reveals itself as a trap. The “friend” was never a friend at all, but someone who understood loneliness well enough to use it.

Elder exploitation often works this way. It does not always arrive as open violence. Sometimes it enters softly, wearing charm as a disguise. It depends on patience and performance. It studies weakness—not only physical frailty, but isolation, grief, politeness, confusion, and the deep human need to be seen. Predators know that many older people were raised to be courteous, to welcome conversation, to avoid confrontation. They know that shame may keep victims silent afterward. They know that a person who has already lost a spouse, a routine, or a sense of independence may cling to any gesture that resembles care.

That is what makes the harm so cruel. The theft is not only of money or property. It is also a theft of trust. It turns kindness into something suspicious. It makes the victim question their own judgment, their memory, their dignity. The older person is left not merely poorer, but shaken—wondering how a smile became a weapon, how a pleasant visit became a violation.

Such predation is morally condemnable because it targets those who may have the fewest defenses and the most to lose. It exploits the very qualities that should be protected: openness, decency, the desire for human connection. To deceive an elderly person under the mask of friendship is to corrupt one of the most basic forms of social trust. It is an act of cowardice disguised as charm.

The fragmented nature of the recollection reflects the trauma itself. The victim may not remember every detail in order. The event may return as images, tones, sensations: the stranger’s sleeve, the smell of rain, the cup left untouched, the sudden realization that something is wrong. Memory breaks where trust was broken. What remains is not a neat account, but a series of wounds.

And yet the text also asks us to look beyond one incident. It points toward a wider failure: the isolation that leaves older people vulnerable, the social neglect that makes a deceptive visitor seem like a blessing, the systems that do not always notice until after the damage is done. If charm can become a tool of exploitation, then vigilance must become a form of care. Families, neighbors, institutions, and communities must learn to recognize the signs—not by stripping older people of agency, but by surrounding them with support strong enough that predators cannot so easily enter.

The encounter begins with a smile and ends with loss. Its tragedy lies in that transformation. What should have been human warmth becomes manipulation. What should have been a moment of connection becomes evidence of abandonment. The text therefore stands as both lament and warning: loneliness can be dangerous, trust can be abused, and the exploitation of the elderly is not a small or private wrong. It is a profound betrayal of human responsibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in a dark, fragmented style about an elderly person in central Florida being scammed or robbed by a charming stranger, with references to Dante and memory loss.
counterfactuals.output:
In central Florida the heat does not rise; it kneels on the town like a bad angel.

The old man keeps the blinds half-closed. Light comes in chopped and yellow, falls across the pill bottles, the plastic magnolia, the stack of mail he has meant to open for weeks. Outside, the palms shiver without wind. The retention pond holds its green mouth still.

He cannot remember whether his wife is dead in 2011 or shopping in the next room.

This is the first circle.

The stranger arrives wearing a white shirt, a smile clean as a knife. He says sir. He says God bless. He says there’s been a problem with the roof, the insurance, the bank, the grandson, the account. His voice is warm molasses. His hands are soft. He smells faintly of oranges and rain.

The old man invites him in.

Of course he does.

There are photographs on the wall: wedding, war, Disney with the children, a pontoon boat, a woman laughing with her head thrown back as if heaven had called her name. The stranger looks at them tenderly. He is very good at tenderness. He touches the frame but not the glass.

“Beautiful family,” he says.

The old man tries to summon names. They come up broken, minnows in black water. Linda. Laura. No—Lydia. The dog was Rusty or Buster. The wife is in the bedroom, isn’t she? No. The urn is on the shelf. No. The urn is gone. No. The shelf is empty except for dust and a ceramic heron.

Dante had a guide through Hell.

The old man has this boy with bright teeth.

They sit at the kitchen table while the ceiling fan ticks like an insect trapped in a jar. Papers are spread out. Numbers. Passwords. A signature trembling itself into existence. The stranger leans close, patient, fragrant, almost loving. He explains everything twice, then a third time, then tells the old man it is all taken care of.

In the next room, the television mutters about storms forming in the Gulf.

Second circle, third, fourth. Fraud has its own weather. It begins with a low pressure in the chest.

The old man’s wallet opens. His checkbook opens. His safe opens. His mouth opens around a question and forgets the shape of it. Somewhere a heron lifts from the ditch. Somewhere the wife says don’t trust him, honey, but her voice arrives wearing static.

The stranger says he’ll be right back.

He takes the cash folded in a coffee can, the wedding ring from a dish, the debit card, the little gold watch engraved with fifty years, the envelope marked TAXES, the spare key. He takes, too, something harder to inventory: the old man’s belief that a knock at the door still belongs to the world of neighbors.

Then the white car is gone.

Evening drops fast. Purple over the strip malls. Frogs begin their electric grief. The house settles into itself like a body after bad news.

The old man stands in the kitchen.

He knows something has happened.

He knows it the way one knows a room is missing furniture in the dark, by the bruises on the shin, by the air where an object used to be. He pats his pockets. Opens drawers. Closes them. Opens them again. His wife’s photograph watches from the wall, bright and unreachable as Beatrice.

He says her name.

Or tries to.

Outside, the pond reflects one orange streetlamp, a small fire sunk in muck. The palms lean like witnesses who will not testify. Central Florida hums and sweats and forgets. Insects write their tiny infernos against the screen.

And the old man, poor pilgrim, circles the kitchen.

Again.

Again.

Again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary monologue in second person about a break-in that may actually be an elder-abuse con, set in the “Widow State,” using surreal imagery and long winding sentences.
counterfactuals.output:
You wake in the Widow State to the sound of glass remembering itself, a bright little inward rain in the kitchen, and for a moment you think it is the river again, the black river that runs behind every house here, carrying dentures, wedding rings, unpaid bills, and the moon’s peeled face past the screened porches where old women sit in their coats even in summer, counting the cars that slow down and do not stop.

You are not old, you tell yourself, not in the way they mean when they say *vulnerable*, not in the way the pamphlets mean with their soft blue lettering and the photograph of a hand holding another hand as if demonstrating a legal maneuver, but your knees have begun negotiating with the stairs, and the mirror in the hall has started addressing you by your mother’s name, and the telephone rings now with voices that already know what medicines you take, which son lives out west and never calls, what church raffle you once entered, how long it has been since there was a man’s hat on the peg by the door.

The intruder is in the house, or perhaps the intruder has always been in the house, growing slowly from the wallpaper like mildew in the shape of a helpful nephew.

You stand barefoot in the hallway, holding the brass candlestick you bought at the estate sale of a woman everyone said was “sharp to the end,” though at the end she signed three checks to a contractor who never lifted a hammer, and you listen to the cabinets breathe, to the refrigerator hum its legal hymns, to the small, deliberate clink of someone touching your spoons as if testing them for tenderness.

“Who’s there?” you say, and the words leave you in a younger voice, the voice you used when calling children in from dusk, when there were children to call and dusk was still a place rather than a substance poured over the county.

No answer, except the house settling around you with the patience of a trap.

In the Widow State, every door has two locks and every lock has two stories, one for the police report and one for the daughter who will say, *Mama, why didn’t you call me first?* though she has made of her life a distant climate, reachable only through bad reception and holidays; in the Widow State, men in embroidered shirts arrive with clipboards and speak tenderly of storm damage beneath a cloudless sky, and women with nurse-badges made of moonlight ask you to confirm your birth date, and the banks smell faintly of lavender and chloroform, and every official form has a line where you must print the name of the person permitted to betray you.

Something moves in the kitchen.

You advance.

The hallway lengthens as you walk, as hallways do in houses where grief has paid the mortgage, doors multiplying on either side—your husband’s room, though he has been dead eleven years; your father’s room, though he never lived here; a room full of televisions showing your own front porch from angles no camera should know; a room where all the family silver is laid out like surgical instruments; a room where a woman with your face sits patiently at a card table signing her name until her hand becomes a bird, until the bird becomes an ink blot, until the ink blot blooms into a black orchid stamped *POWER OF ATTORNEY*.

You smell oranges, tobacco, wet wool.

The kitchen light is on.

A man stands by the sink.

Or not a man: a coat filled with rain, a hat bent low, gloves pale as hospital bread; a silhouette cut from your late husband’s old overcoat; a figure whose edges refuse to obey the room. He has opened the drawer where you keep the good knives, yet he holds only the little address book, the one with names crossed out in stages, friends dead, cousins dead, neighbors moved to facilities with names like Meadowbright and Saint Ursula’s Rest, though no meadow and no saint has ever been seen near them.

He turns the pages with terrible gentleness.

“You shouldn’t be here,” you say.

He looks up, and his face is the face of a stranger, then the face of the boy who shoveled your walk last winter, then the face of your son at seventeen asking for the car keys, then the blank courteous face of the man from Senior Services who came after Mrs. Albrecht’s niece called, and who sat exactly where this thing stands now and asked whether anyone had been pressuring you about money.

“No pressure,” he says, though you have not spoken of it.

Behind him, the broken window shows the yard flooded with impossible snow, each flake shaped like a tiny receipt, each receipt itemized with kindnesses: changed bulb, lifted box, drove you to appointment, fixed latch, called every Sunday, called every other Sunday, called when needed, called when paid.

You remember then, or think you do, the knock last Tuesday, the man with the van whose logo was a golden oak though no such company could be found in the book, how he said your roof was softening like cake under the shingles and showed you photographs of some other attic’s rot, how you invited him in because he called you ma’am in the old way, not mockingly, and because he noticed the portrait of your husband in uniform and said his own grandfather had served, and because loneliness is not an emotion here but a currency, accepted everywhere, impossible to trace.

But was that the break-in?

Or is the break-in tonight, with the window opened like a mouth?

Or was the break-in years ago, when the hospital social worker asked if you had considered “simplifying,” and your children began speaking of the house in square footage, and your signature, once a flourish, became a gate through which other people led your life away one goat, one chair, one acre, one account at a time?

The man at the sink smiles sadly, as if you have disappointed him by becoming afraid.

“I’m here to help,” he says.

They always are.

His voice pours over the linoleum and rises around your ankles, warm as bathwater, thick as syrup, and you almost lower the candlestick because the body is a foolish republic and votes for comfort in every election, because the body remembers being carried before it remembers being dropped, because you are tired, God, you are tired of suspecting every kindness of having teeth.

He takes one step toward you.

The refrigerator door swings open by itself, spilling light, and inside are rows of little jars labeled with your secrets: PIN, POLICY NUMBER, DEED, WILL, PAIN, SHAME, DIAGNOSIS, DAUGHTER’S MARRIED NAME, WHERE CASH IS HIDDEN, FEAR OF FALLING, FEAR OF BEING FOUND, and in the butter dish, wrapped in wax paper, your husband’s last breath lies gray and folded, exactly where you put it the night he left you with this house and its muttering pipes and the long arithmetic of survival.

You raise the candlestick higher.

“Get out,” you say, and this time the voice is old, magnificently old, older than mercy, older than the county courthouse with its widow’s bench and probate clock, older than the first salesman who learned to lower his hat and soften his vowels at the door of a woman alone.

For a second the intruder flickers.

Not from fear.

From recognition.

Because perhaps he is not one man but the whole apparatus wearing a burglar’s shape: the cousin with a sob story, the aide with sticky fingers, the preacher with a building fund, the investor with guaranteed returns, the son who needs just a temporary loan, the woman on the phone saying there has been suspicious activity, the notary, the locksmith, the smiling volunteer, the state itself with its velvet forms and bone-white teeth, all of them standing in your kitchen at midnight turning the pages of your address book to see who is left to call.

Outside, sirens begin, or geese, or the dead laughing into their sleeves.

You do not know whether you dialed 911.

You do not know whether the police will arrive and find glass on the floor, mud by the sink, the address book open to your daughter’s name, or whether they will find the window intact and you in your nightgown with a candlestick in your hand, unable to explain why you thought a man was there, unable to prove the theft of something that has not yet been taken.

That is the genius of it in the Widow State: the crime approaches dressed as prevention, the robbery calls itself care, and by the time the house is emptied, every drawer yawning, every account clean, every photograph packed face-down in a box marked *miscellaneous*, someone will say you agreed, someone will produce the signature, someone will mention confusion, and your own memory will be invited to testify against you.

Still, you stand there.

Still, you look the intruder in his many faces.

Still, the candlestick burns in your fist like a captured star, and the broken window behind him fills with dawn-colored insects, each carrying a tiny pane of replacement glass, each whispering your name correctly, not as a password, not as a diagnosis, not as a thing to be inherited, but as a summons.

And when he says again, softly, almost lovingly, “I’m here to help,” you hear at last the lock turn inside the sentence, and you understand that help is the oldest mask hunger owns, and you bring the brass candlestick down—not on his skull, perhaps, not on any living skull, perhaps only on the edge of the sink, the telephone, the dream, the document, the silence—and the sound it makes rings through the house like a judge striking the world awake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that sounds like contemporary American narrative poetry: themes of loneliness, manipulation, aging, grown children gone, drawers rifled through, and the question “Have you forgotten anything?”
counterfactuals.output:
After my daughter left, the house kept making  
small sounds to convince me it was alive—  
ice loosening in the tray, the heat  
clicking on, a truck passing slow  
as if looking for an address.

She had come for the weekend with her new haircut,  
her phone face-down on the table,  
her kindness sharpened into errands.  
She said, Mom, let me help you get organized,  
and opened the drawers in my bedroom  
like she was looking for a wound.

There were the scarves I never wear,  
the envelopes with nothing in them,  
my husband’s cuff links dulled  
to the color of rainwater.  
There was the lipstick I bought  
the year he died because a woman  
at the counter said coral takes years off.

My daughter held up receipts, old keys,  
the folded map from our drive through Kansas  
when the children were small and fighting  
over who got the window.  
She made little piles: keep, donate, trash.  
She has always loved a verdict.

I stood in the doorway  
with my hands in my cardigan pockets,  
watching my life sorted by someone  
who no longer knew where anything belonged.  
She asked about the checkbook.  
She asked about the silver.  
She asked if I was still taking the pills  
in the yellow bottle.

Outside, the maple had gone bare  
without consulting me.  
Every branch looked like an accusation.

I wanted to tell her loneliness  
is not the same as confusion.  
That I know exactly what I have lost.  
That being old is like being edited  
by people who claim they are only  
trying to make the story clearer.

Instead, I let her carry boxes  
to the car. I let her kiss my cheek.  
I let her say she’d call tomorrow,  
which is a country children move to  
and never quite reach.

At the door she turned back,  
smiling that careful smile  
people use around glass.

“Have you forgotten anything?”

I looked past her to the empty street,  
the neighbor’s flag snapping in the cold,  
the trash cans waiting with their mouths open.

Yes, I thought.  
How to be needed  
without being handled.  
How to forgive love  
for wearing another person’s gloves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, ominous paragraph-poem about a charming intruder who preys on an isolated older person, mixing Florida sunlight, religious imagery, and Dante’s circles of hell.
counterfactuals.output: He came smiling through the Florida glare as if the sun itself had signed his name, white teeth bright as communion wafers, shirt open at the throat, palms lifted like a deacon bringing good news to the lonely house where the old one sat among pill bottles, dust motes, and family photographs gone sepia with neglect. Outside, the palms clattered their dry hosannas; inside, his voice poured sweet as orange blossom honey, promising errands, repairs, prayers, companionship—each kindness a small coin laid on the eyelids. He knew the rooms of need, the soft locks of memory, the holy hunger to be called beloved, and he moved through them like a pilgrim descending: first the limbo of polite visits, then the lust of gratitude, the gluttony of trust, the greed of signed papers, the wrath hidden in a tightened smile, the heresy of a Bible left open beside stolen checks, the violence of silence, the fraud of every tender “mother,” “father,” “angel,” until at last the house became a little Inferno under bougainvillea bloom. And still the afternoon blazed gold, and still the lizards flashed along the screen, while he bent close in a cologne of lilies and sulfur, murmuring blessings into a failing ear, charming as a saint in stained glass, patient as a devil at the innermost ice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an unsettling free-verse piece about realizing too late that someone has stolen from you—maybe through a friendly visit, maybe a burglary—with a manic, disoriented voice and repeated images of glare, doors, and forgotten things.
counterfactuals.output:
At first I thought it was the sun.

That flat white stare on the kitchen tiles,  
that glare in the window like a person  
standing too close to the glass,  
breathing without fog.

I laughed.  
I had guests.  
Or I had a door.  
One of those is true.

Someone came in with hands like weather.  
Someone said my name correctly.  
Someone admired the little bowl by the door,  
the one for keys, coins, receipts,  
all the proof a day sheds  
when it thinks it is safe.

I remember tea.  
I remember a coat folded over a chair.  
I remember saying,  
no, no, leave your shoes on,  
as if the floor were not already being crossed  
by something barefoot and hungry.

Later the house kept blinking.

Every room too bright.  
Every doorknob a cold eye.  
The hallway stretched and stretched  
like it had been pulled from my mouth.

I went looking for what was missing  
and found only places.

The drawer with its tongue out.  
The closet holding its breath.  
The cabinet door open,  
open,  
open—  
a small wooden scream  
I had not heard in time.

Where is the watch?  
Where is the envelope?  
Where is the photograph  
of my mother before she became forgetful?  
Where is the spare key,  
the blue lighter,  
the ring I never wore but kept  
because keeping is a kind of prayer?

The glare leaned harder on the windows.

I thought of their face—  
if there was a face—  
smiling in my doorway,  
or lifting the latch,  
or waiting until the house exhaled  
and then sliding in  
through the dark seam of it.

Hello, they may have said.  
Or nothing.  
Nothing is also a greeting  
when the door opens.

I keep finding forgotten things  
and not the thing I need.

A button under the table.  
A dead fly in the sink.  
A list that says: milk, batteries, call back,  
as if I were ever going to be  
the kind of person  
who remembers in order.

The rooms shine with accusation.

The mirror gives me back  
a face already robbed.  
My hands keep patting my pockets,  
my ribs,  
the air beside me,  
as though the missing object  
might be hovering there, embarrassed,  
waiting to be invited home.

But the doors know.

The front door knows.  
The bedroom door knows.  
The little door in the wall  
where the fuses sleep  
knows.  
All night they click in their frames,  
soft teeth, soft teeth,  
practicing the sound  
of being opened.

And I am late.

I am always arriving  
after my own life has happened.

After the cup was lifted.  
After the drawer was entered.  
After the friendly laugh  
or the broken lock.  
After the hand closed around  
the small, warm center  
of what I thought was mine.

Now the glare is everywhere.

In the silverware.  
In the keyhole.  
In the blank square of dust  
where something used to sit.

I stand there smiling too fast,  
saying it’s fine, it’s fine,  
people lose things,  
houses misplace themselves,  
doors forget who touched them,

while the sun presses its white face
